songs.name: I'm A Hog For You Baby

ai_show_review.summary: Pigpen‑driven R&B set with stellar Hog For You and Hey Little One
ai_show_review.blurb: The show showcases Ron Pigpen’s thunderous organ leading an early‑Dead R&B groove. Highlights include “I’m A Hog For You Baby,” “Hey Little One,” and a tight rendition of “Cold Rain And Snow.” Jerry’s vocals are raw and passionate while the rhythm section drives solidly.
ai_show_review.review:
On March 25, 1966 at the Trouper's Club in Los Angeles the Grateful Dead delivered a classic early‑Dead R&B set that is dominated by Ron "Pigpen" McKernan’s organ. The matrix recording (gd66-03-25.sbd.unknown.38.sbeok.shnf) is remarkably clear – vocals sit on one channel while the instruments occupy the other, giving listeners an almost stage‑side feel. Pigpen’s organ is “thunderous” and occasionally overpowers the mix, but it fuels standout moments like “I’m A Hog For You Baby,” “Hey Little One,” and the soulful “Cold Rain And Snow.” Jerry Garcia’s guitar slips out of tune at times, yet his passionate singing and fiery riffs cut through, especially on “You Don't Have To Ask.” Phil Lesh provides a solid bass foundation even though it sits slightly recessed, and Bill Kreutzmann drives the groove; a brief kick‑drum distortion appears on “Next Time You See Me” but disappears when summed to mono. Overall the performance feels cohesive, raw, and historically exciting – a true snapshot of the band’s early sound.

The second recording (gd1966-03-25.139750.sbd.miller.clugston.flac1648) is described as “raw” and historic, with Jerry’s voice highlighted as pure, but it lacks the clarity of the matrix source. For anyone wanting to experience this formative era, the matrix tape remains the definitive listening choice.

best_recording.reason: Clear split‑channel matrix capture; organ is front‑and‑center, overall sound is listenable despite minor mix quirks.

key_highlights: Thunderous Pigpen organ leading the R&B set.
"I’m A Hog For You Baby" and "Hey Little One" stand out as organ‑driven showcases.
Jerry’s raw, passionate vocals cut through even with occasional guitar tuning issues.
Solid rhythm section foundation from Phil and Bill despite a brief kick‑drum distortion.
